items.stem: An urgent email from a 'manager' asks you to change a supplier's bank details immediately. What is the safest action?

options.text: Verify the request out of band using a known contact method before acting
options.rationale: Correct: out-of-band verification defeats business email compromise.

options.text: Change the details right away to avoid delay
options.rationale: Acting on urgency without verification is the attacker's goal.

options.text: Reply to the email to confirm
options.rationale: Replying may just reach the attacker who controls the thread.

options.text: Ignore it entirely and tell no one
options.rationale: Ignoring without reporting leaves others exposed.

items.explanation: Correct: verify out of band through a known channel before acting.

items.stem: Which TWO are common psychological triggers used in social engineering? (Select TWO.)

options.rationale: Correct: urgency pushes targets to act without thinking.

options.text: Apparent authority, such as posing as a manager
options.rationale: Correct: authority discourages questioning the request.

options.text: Offering to slow the process down for careful review
options.rationale: Attackers avoid giving time for scrutiny.

options.text: Encouraging the target to verify independently

items.explanation: Correct: urgency and apparent authority are classic triggers.

items.stem: Why is caller ID not sufficient proof of a caller's identity?

options.text: Caller ID can be spoofed to display any number
options.rationale: Correct: displayed numbers can be forged, so they do not prove identity.
Caller ID often shows a number; the issue is it can be faked.
Phones do display numbers; they simply can be spoofed.
Spoofing is not limited to mobile phones.

items.explanation: Correct: caller ID can be spoofed and does not prove identity.
